$comment: What every key on the page is for. Sections describe where a group of strings appears; notes single out the ones constrained by something other than meaning. Read with GLOSSARY.md.

sections.meta: Never seen on the page. These are the search result, the browser tab, and the card that appears when the address is pasted into a chat application. Written for someone who has not heard of Lukotta.
sections.ui: Controls in the header, and the link that lets a keyboard reader skip the navigation. Read aloud by screen readers, so they must say what the control does rather than name it cleverly.
sections.nav: The three header links. Each matches a heading further down and should use the same words as that heading.
sections.hero: The first screen. One claim, one sentence explaining it, the download link, and a technical line set in a monospace face.
sections.features: Section 01, in prose. What the application is for, said in plain sentences rather than a list of bullet points.
sections.extras: Seven short entries under section 01: a heading of two or three words and one sentence. These are the things worth knowing that did not belong in the prose.
sections.formats: Section 02. A single table of everything the application opens, grouped into encryption, filesystems and disk images, with a Read and a Write column. The table is the reason many readers come to the page.
sections.how: Section 03. Why a Linux virtual machine is involved, three steps, and what the application asks the reader's Mac for.
sections.download: The closing section: the call to action and what a Mac needs before the application will run.
sections.footer: Three links, and the copyright and licence line beneath them.
sections.faq: Nine questions, written the way a reader would type them into a search engine. These are published as structured data as well as shown on the page, so a search engine may show a question and its answer directly in its results. Every answer must stand on its own, without the question.
sections.name: Section 04, where the name is explained. Set as a dictionary entry: the word itself large, the language and the meaning beside it, then two short sentences. Taken from the application's own README.
sections.story: Section 06, after the questions: why the application was written, in the author's own voice and in the first person. Four paragraphs of ordinary prose, no lists and no headings inside it. The tone is level and unsentimental — it argues that encrypting a drive is ordinary and that being unable to open it elsewhere is what stops people. It should not read as marketing, and it should not frighten anybody.

notes.meta.title: At or under 60 characters. Search results cut it off. Keyword first, brand last.
notes.meta.description: Between 70 and 165 characters. Longer is truncated mid-word.
notes.meta.ogTitle: The card title when the address is shared. May be shorter and less formal than meta.title.
notes.meta.imageAlt: Describes the Lukotta application icon, which is the shared card image.
notes.ui.skipToContent: The first thing a keyboard reader reaches. Must say plainly that it skips to the page content.
notes.ui.toTop: The spoken name of the logo, which is a link back to the top of the page.
notes.ui.switchToLight: The appearance switch's spoken name while the page is dark. It names what clicking will do, not what the page currently is.
notes.ui.switchToDark: The same switch while the page is light.
notes.hero.title: The one sentence the page is built around. Keep the full stop.
notes.hero.meta: Set in a monospace face at a small size. Contains {version}, which becomes the released version number. Keep the middle dots as separators, and leave GPL-3.0-or-later exactly as it is.
notes.features.lead: The opening claim, and the only place the page says what macOS does wrong. Plain, not indignant.
notes.features.body: Says the drive is opened in place and nothing is converted or copied. This is a factual claim about how the application works; do not strengthen it.
notes.extras.title: A one-word heading joining the prose above to the seven entries below. Set in a monospace face, in capitals. If the language has no natural single word here, a short phrase is fine.
notes.extras.1.def: Read-only is enforced in two places, inside the virtual machine and on the Mac. Both halves matter and both should survive.
notes.extras.6.term: The number of languages. Update it here if the count changes.
notes.extras.7.def: Bin is Apple's word for where a deleted application goes. Use whatever the reader's Mac calls it.
notes.formats.lead: Introduces the table. The phrase 'will and will not write' is deliberate: the table has rows that are read but never written.
notes.formats.col.read: A column heading, set in capitals in a monospace face. One word if the language allows.
notes.formats.col.write: The same. These two headings sit above columns of ticks and dashes.
notes.formats.yes: Never shown on screen. It is the spoken text behind a tick, for a reader using a screen reader.
notes.formats.vmdkStream.note: Explains why this one format is read but not written. Factual, not a warning.
notes.formats.vhdx.note: The same. The application says so before the image opens, which is worth keeping.
notes.formats.specs: The whole string is a link to SPECS.md. It reads as a sentence, not as a button.
notes.formats.not.body: A list of what cannot be opened, separated by full stops. Each item is a distinct reason; keep them distinct.
notes.how.lead: The whole explanation in three sentences: macOS cannot, Linux can, so a small Linux machine does it.
notes.how.1.body: Contains menu paths written with an arrow: File → Open Disk Image. Use the arrow, and Apple's own names for the File menu in this language.
notes.how.note: Explains why the drive shows a network icon in Finder. Reassurance, so it must not sound like an apology or a defect.
notes.how.permissions.1: Full Disk Access, exactly as System Settings names it in this language.
notes.how.permissions.3: The claim that Lukotta never sees the administrator password is precise and load-bearing. Translate it exactly.
notes.download.body: Carries the privacy claim — collects nothing, no account, one update check. Do not strengthen it beyond the English.
notes.download.req.1: Says plainly that Intel Macs are not supported. Do not soften it; a reader on an Intel Mac needs to know before downloading.
notes.footer.copyright: Contains {year}, replaced when the page is built, and {author}, which becomes a link to the author's own site. Both must survive, spelled exactly as they are.
notes.footer.gpl: The licence line. GNU General Public License is a proper name and is not translated, though the surrounding sentence is.
notes.faq.1.a: Names the GNU General Public License, which is not translated.
notes.faq.2.q: Phrased as a search. Keep BitLocker and Mac in it — those are the words a reader would use.
notes.faq.3.a: The distinction between what macOS does (read-only) and what Lukotta does (read and write) is the whole answer. Keep both halves.
notes.faq.5.q: Long, and deliberately so: it is the question people actually ask.
notes.faq.6.a: Says plainly that Intel Macs are not supported. Do not soften it.
notes.faq.7.a: A safety claim. Do not strengthen it beyond the English, and do not weaken it either.
notes.name.gloss: What Lúkotta means, translated into this language. It is shown in quotation marks; use the quotation marks this language uses.
notes.name.body: Contains {lukko} and {tta}, which become the Finnish word lukko and the Finnish ending -tta. Both are Finnish and stay as they are in every language; the placeholders must survive, spelled exactly as they are, and the sentence around them is translated.
notes.name.stress: About where the stress falls when the word is said aloud. The page shows this by setting the first syllable apart, so the sentence and the picture must agree.
notes.name.language: The name of the Finnish language in this language.
notes.story.1: About why a drive is worth locking at all. Concrete and calm: a bag, a drawer, a sold machine. Do not sharpen this into a warning.
notes.story.2: The argument the whole section rests on: people leave drives unlocked because a locked one will not open on their other machine. Keep the reasoning intact even if the sentences are rebuilt.
notes.story.3: About terminal utilities. It respects the people who use them and says they are not an answer for everybody. Keep both halves; dropping the first turns a fair point into a sneer.
notes.story.4: First person, and the only place on the page where the author speaks as himself. Keep it in the first person in every language.
notes.story.signature: Just {author}, which becomes the author's name. Nothing to translate; the placeholder must survive exactly as it is.
